title: Indie and the Woad Wonder
markdown:
It was during those long school holidays that stretched out like a lazy cat in the sunshine. No homework in sight. Indie the ink-maker and Thistle the moor pony were two chums who found a secret hiding in plain sight, a secret that painted their holiday the most astonishing blue.

Indie wasn’t just any ink-maker. Her tiny workshop, tucked away at the edge of the village, smelled of lavender and damp earth. Her inks were pure craft. She made shimmering emerald greens from moss gathered after a rain shower and fiery oranges from marigolds picked at dawn.

And Thistle? A stout shaggy chap, the colour of a stormy sky just before thunder. His eyes twinkled like distant stars. He could carry Indie across bumpy fields and through rustling woods with a steady sway, his mane a wild dark cloud.

One bright morning, the kind that makes you want to hum, they were trotting towards their favourite spot by the Whispering Brook. A ribbon of green leading to a little stream. Smooth grey stepping stones made hopping across easy. But as they rounded the bend, Indie stopped Thistle with a gentle nudge.

“Hold on, Thistle. Look.”

Across the familiar moss-kissed stones, there were splotches. Not just any splotches: bright bold splashes of the most incredible vibrant blue. They shimmered, almost alive, against the grey rock, like tiny fallen pieces of the sky.

Indie’s eyes widened. She noticed everything. The way a dewdrop caught the light, turning it into a miniature rainbow. The intricate pattern on a beetle’s shell. And these blue splotches? A puzzle. A splash of the unexpected.

“That’s odd,” she murmured, brow furrowed just a tiny bit. She looked at Thistle, who blinked his big gentle eyes. “These weren’t here yesterday, were they, Thistle?”

Indie, ink-stained fingers tingling with questions, hopped off Thistle. She crouched, knees sinking slightly into the soft grass, examining the blue. It was unlike any blue she’d ever mixed. It had a depth, a liveliness, that her carefully crafted inks couldn’t quite capture. It felt wild.

“It’s not paint,” she decided, touching it gently with a fingertip. Cool and slightly damp, like morning mist. “And it’s not berry juice. It’s something else.” A flutter danced in her tummy, the exciting sort that nudged you towards discovery.

Thistle, ever patient, snorted softly, nudging her with his velvety nose. He was always ready for wherever these blue clues led, tail giving a little encouraging swish.

Indie stood up, a grin spreading. “Well, Thistle, it looks like our holiday just got a whole lot more colourful.”

They followed the trail of blue splotches, each one a little beacon guiding them deeper into the woods. The path wound and twisted, leading them away from the familiar babbling of the brook and into a quieter mossier part of the forest, where sunlight dappled through ancient leaves.

The blue spots led them past a sleepy badger’s sett, where a little black and white nose poked out for a moment before disappearing again. They ducked under a canopy of ancient oak trees, branches gnarled like old wizards’ fingers. Thistle, with his keen senses, would often nudge Indie in the right direction when the splotches seemed to fade, as if he could smell the colour on the breeze.

“You’re a clever pony, Thistle,” Indie would praise, scratching his shaggy neck, feeling the warmth of his fur.

Then they stumbled upon it. Hidden away in a sun-dappled clearing, bathed in golden light, was a patch of plants. And on their leaves, tiny droplets of that same astonishing blue. The plants were slender, with long lance-shaped leaves and small delicate flowers just starting to bloom, like tiny sky-blue bells.

“Woad,” Indie gasped, breath catching. She’d read about it in one of her dusty old books, a forgotten treasure from long ago. A plant used for making dye, a deep beautiful blue that coloured fabrics for royalty and knights. But it was rarely seen nowadays.

“It’s incredible,” she whispered, touching a leaf very carefully. “Look, Thistle, the colour is seeping right into the stone here, like it’s leaving a message.”

Thistle gave a soft whinny, ears pricked.

As Indie looked closer, she noticed that while the splotches on the stones were vibrant, the colour on the plants themselves seemed a little faded. The magic felt like it was slowly slipping away, like a colour fading in the sun.

“Oh no,” Indie said, voice tinged with worry. She looked from the vibrant blue on the stones to the slightly duller leaves. “It’s like the colour is disappearing. If we don’t figure out how to help it, this beautiful blue might be gone forever.”

She could simply marvel at the woad, perhaps pick a few leaves to press in her journal, and be on her way. Or she could try to help preserve this fading wonder. It was tempting to just observe, to let it drift away like dandelion fluff. But Indie, the girl who saw the world as a palette waiting to be explored, couldn’t bear to see such a magnificent colour vanish.

“We need to help these plants,” she declared, eyes shining with a new kind of determination. She squared her shoulders, a firm set to her jaw.

She thought hard. She knew about inks, about pigments, about how colours needed the right conditions to flourish. She remembered a special gentle way she coaxed the colour out of certain berries for her inks, a method that didn’t damage the fruit, but instead encouraged it to release its most vibrant hue.

“Maybe,” she mused aloud, voice gaining confidence, “if I can carefully extract some of the essence — not to make ink, but to feed the plant itself — to remind it of its own beautiful colour?”

It was a long shot, a real adventure into the unknown. She rummaged in her satchel, gathering her smallest pots and finest brushes, the ones she used for the most delicate lines in her artwork. With the utmost care she began to gently dab at the leaves, collecting the faintest hints of blue. But as she worked, a leaf she’d reached for slipped from its stem and tumbled to the ground. “Oh, bother,” she muttered, a flicker of frustration. She knew she had to be even more precise, even gentler, if this was to work. The air around them seemed to hum. The leaves felt cool beneath her touch. The scent of damp earth filled her nostrils, mixing with the faint sweet perfume of the woad flowers. The blue shimmered on her fingertips, a promise of what could be.

It was slow, painstaking work. Thistle stood nearby, a silent comforting presence, occasionally nudging a fallen leaf closer to Indie’s reach with his nose, his soft breathing a gentle rhythm in the quiet clearing. As Indie meticulously worked, coaxing the faintest whisper of blue from the woad leaves, something happened.

The plants seemed to perk up. The leaves unfurled a little more, reaching towards the dappled sunlight. And the blue droplets on the stepping stones, which had been starting to look a little dull, seemed to catch the light with renewed brilliance, glowing as if they had just been painted.

Indie hummed a little tune, a happy contented sound, fingers moving with a confidence she hadn’t known she possessed. She wasn’t just an ink-maker anymore; she was a colour-keeper.

When the sun began to dip below the trees, painting the sky in orange and pink, Indie finally packed away her tools, her heart full. The patch of woad plants looked healthier, greener, and the blue shimmered with a revived energy.

“We did it, Thistle,” she whispered, patting his warm flank, feeling the steady beat of his heart.

They made their way back along the stepping stones, which now seemed to glow with a soft residual blue, as if they remembered. The splotches were still there, a testament to their discovery, but now they felt like friendly reminders, not urgent mysteries.

Indie looked at her ink-stained hands, then at the woad plants still shimmering in the fading light. She did not bottle the colour. She left it on the stones, on the leaves, on her fingertips. The workshop at the village edge would still smell of lavender tomorrow. The woad, in its clearing, kept its own blue.
